ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: In a certain plant, the pair of relative traits red flower and white flower is simultaneously controlled by multiple pairs of allelic genes (such as A, a; B, b; C c …). Only when each pair of allelic genes in an individual’s genotype contains at least one dominant gene (that is, A_B_C_…) will it bloom red flowers; otherwise it blooms white flowers. There are now four pure-breeding white-flower lines, A, B, C, and D, which are crossed with one another. The crossing combinations, offspring phenotypes, and their ratios are shown in the figure. Answer the question: in this experiment, by how many pairs of allelic genes is the plant flower color controlled?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: the figure lists the crossing results among four pure-breeding white-flower lines, A, B, C, and D. A×B has F1 white and F2 white; A×C has F1 white and F2 white; C×D has F1 white and F2 white. B×C has F1 red and F2 red 81:white 175; A×D has F1 red and F2 red 81:white 175; B×D has F1 red and F2 red 27:white 37. Then reason: the question stem states that only when each pair of allelic genes controlling flower color contains at least one dominant gene, that is, A_B_C_…, will red flowers bloom; otherwise they are white flowers. If an F1 red-flower individual undergoes segregation at n pairs of related genes, then the red-flower proportion in F2 is (3/4)^n. In the figure, the F2 red-flower proportion of B×C and A×D is 81/(81+175)=81/256=(3/4)^4, indicating that 4 pairs of allelic genes participate in segregation and jointly determine the red-flower phenotype. B×D has 27/(27+37)=27/64=(3/4)^3, which is consistent with segregation of 3 of the gene pairs. Therefore, in this experiment, the plant flower color is controlled by 4 pairs of allelic genes.
